item.title: Luan hits 40 years of policing in Lae
item.description: For 40 years, Chief Inspector James Luan has been a familiar face in the police service in Lae. He joined the Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary in 1985 as a young man looking for work. Four decades later, he is still in uniform and has spent his entire police career serving in Lae.
item.content:encoded:
For 40 years, Chief Inspector James Luan has been a familiar face in the police service in Lae.

He joined the Royal Papua New Guinea Constabulary in 1985 as a young man looking for work. Four decades later, he is still in uniform and has spent his entire police career serving in Lae.

“I've been serving in Lae for 40 years. Continuous service in Lae only,” Luan said. “I've never transferred to any parts of Morobe Province, any districts in Morobe, or any other provinces in Papua New Guinea. All my 40 years of service has been in Lae only.”

Luan's entry into the police force was not something he had planned. He completed teachers college in 1984 and was offered a teaching position in Western Highlands province. His parents were concerned about him travelling to the islands and advised him not to take the job. While looking for another opportunity, he noticed that police were recruiting.

“I did not have the ambition to be a police officer. It was just an opportunity that I saw,” he said. “I was looking for a job. When I noticed that they were looking for new police recruits, I just went in there and applied. I got selected and that's where I am now.”

Luan completed six months of basic constable training at Bomana before he was posted to Lae in February 1986. That was the beginning of a career that would see him serve in different police units and stations across the city.

From 1990 to 1996, he served with the Unitech Campus Police. He later worked at Chinatown Police Station, gaining experience in one of Lae's busy urban areas. His career progressed through the ranks. He became a senior constable in 1992, sergeant in 2006, senior sergeant in 2010 and chief sergeant in 2014.

In 2020, he became a senior inspector before being promoted to chief inspector four years after. For Luan, each promotion represented another stage of a career that began almost by chance. As a young constable, he watched senior officers and imagined himself one day wearing the sergeant's rank.

“When I was a constable, I saw a lot of sergeants around wearing this rank and I thought that one day I'll be a sergeant,” he said. “That was the rank that I loved in the force.”

He eventually moved beyond that rank and into the commissioned ranks. But the years in between were not always easy.

“It's a very challenging career. We deal with people. A lot of people come to us with their problems and there are a lot of law and order issues,” he said.

His work also included national election operations.

Luan led police contingents from Lae to the islands during several elections. Throughout those years, he remained based in Lae. He said senior officers he worked under also had an important influence on his career. Their leadership, communication and professionalism helped shape the way he approached his own work.

After four decades in the police force, Luan said discipline and humility are among the important lessons he has learnt. He also wants younger officers to understand that difficult working conditions should not stop them from serving the public.

“You might have ups and downs. You don't have resources, you might not have logistics, but do whatever you can to serve the people,” he said. “The service is more important.”

For Luan, serving people also means having a good relationship with the communities. He believes police officers need to spend time talking to people, listening to their concerns and working with them to find solutions.

“We need to work closely with the communities, talk to them, sit down with them, hear their problems and find some solutions,” he said. “That's all about working together in partnership.”

Luan started his police career when he was about 20. He had not planned to become a policeman. He was simply looking for a job after deciding not to take up his teaching appointment. That decision led him to Bomana, then to Lae, where he would spend the next 40 years.

From senior constable to sergeant, senior sergeant, chief sergeant, senior inspector and now chief inspector, his career has moved forward while his posting has remained the same.

Lae has been the only place he has known as a policeman. For four decades, James Luan has continued to serve the city he first arrived in as a young constable.

item.title: Vanuatu police to train at PNG Center of Excellence
item.description: A delegation from the Vanuatu police force have been welcomed as preparations continue for Vanuatu police recruits to undertake training at the PNG Centre of Excellence at Bomana next year. 50 Vanuatu police recruits will undertake a six-month program at Bomana next year, delivered jointly by instructors from Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu.
item.content:encoded:
A delegation from the Vanuatu police force have been welcomed as preparations continue for Vanuatu police recruits to undertake training at the PNG Centre of Excellence at Bomana next year.

50 Vanuatu police recruits will undertake a six-month program at Bomana next year, delivered jointly by instructors from Papua New Guinea and Vanuatu.

Police Commissioner David Manning said that, by training alongside RPNGC personnel, the Vanuatu recruits will strengthen domestic policing skills, deepen their understanding of cross-border law enforcement and establish professional networks that can be called upon during future regional operations.

“The Pacific is facing increasingly complex threats from transnational criminal organisations who seek to exploit vulnerabilities across our region.

“Pacific police forces are working together to prevent our countries from being used as transit points for illicit drugs, weapons, laundered money, human trafficking and other organised criminal activity.” Commissioner Manning said.

Manning said, Papua New Guinea’s policing relationship with Australia is now deepened with operational partnerships, including Vanuatu.

Commissioner Manning said the RPNGC–Vanuatu recruit training program, discussed by Police Ministers in Port Vila in July this year, would strengthen the professional skills of Vanuatu Police Force recruits while building lasting operational relationships between the two police forces.

He said the benefits flowing from the RPNGC–Vanuatu recruit program shows the wider potential of Pacific police forces working together as the region moves forward.

item.title: 2 vice ministries added to current cabinet
item.description: Prime Minister James Marape has appointed two new vice ministters to the Marape – Rosso Cabinet , a move to develop young leadership for the country. They are Usino Bundi MP Vincent Kumura as vice minister assisting the Office of the Prime Minister and Pogera Paiela MP Gidron Karipe as Vice Minister Petroleum.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister James Marape has appointed two new vice ministters to the Marape – Rosso Cabinet , a move to develop young leadership for the country.

They are Usino Bundi MP Vincent Kumura as vice minister assisting the Office of the Prime Minister and Pogera Paiela MP Gidron Karipe as Vice Minister Petroleum.

Both were sworn in by Governor General Sir Bob Dadae at the government house, witnessed by several senior state ministers.

Speaking to the media, Marape says the appointments are part of his independence message to the nation about nurturing the next generation of leaders.

‘"I thank all other senior ministers and members of Parliament who showed up to pay respect to the bleeding and breeding of the next generation of leadership. Symbolic indication: the first day after the 16th of September, we just had to sign it out," the prime minister said.2

Consistent with my division of our country into three population groupings, those of us above 50, part of our job also is to breed those who are in between 26 to 50, to be at work correctly for our country."

Both Kumura and Karipe thanked Prime Minister James Marape for his confidence, saying they would work to fulfil their responsibilities until the 2027 national elections.

item.title: Doctor dies after alleged assault in Kundiawa
item.description: A 26-year-old medical officer serving at the Sir Joseph Nombri Memorial Kundiawa Provincial Hospital has died after an alleged brutal assault, casting a dark shadow over Papua New Guinea's 51st Independence Day celebrations in Simbu. The deceased is Dr Robert Waiye from Gera village in the Sinesine Yongomugl District.
item.content:encoded:
A 26-year-old medical officer serving at the Sir Joseph Nombri Memorial Kundiawa Provincial Hospital has died after an alleged brutal assault, casting a dark shadow over Papua New Guinea's 51st Independence Day celebrations in Simbu.

The deceased is Dr Robert Waiye from Gera village in the Sinesine Yongomugl District.

Simbu Provincial Police Commander, Chief Superintendent Mazuc Rubiang, confirmed the incident.

PPC Rubiang said seven suspects, including another doctor, are now in police custody.

He assured the family, hospital staff and the people of Simbu that police will get to the bottom of the investigation and that those involved will face the full force of the law.

Dr Waiye allegedly sustained severe traumatic brain injury after being attacked between 12:30 am and 2:00 am on Wednesday, September 16, 2026, at the residence of the owner of Gateway Fuelers Club at DPI, Kundiawa.

According to eyewitnesses, Dr Waiye and a colleague had drinks at the club and were leaving when they were allegedly attacked by youths who were drinking inside the club owner's residence.

He was rushed to the hospital, where colleagues and specialist doctors attempted urgent interventions, but he succumbed to his injuries and was pronounced dead at 8:38 am today (Thursday, September 17, 2026).

PPC Rubiang described the incident as 'animalistic and barbaric'.

Following the death, the Simbu Provincial Health Authority [SiPHA] issued a petition to the Provincial Police Commander, with instructions to deliver it to all mandated leaders in the six districts of Simbu, including the Governor.

SiPHA CEO, Dr Ken Kassi, condemned the killing in the strongest terms imaginable, saying it is unacceptable for a Simbu doctor to die at the hands of fellow Simbus.

In the petition SiPHA outlined three key demands:

Dr Kassi emphasized that Simbu's doctor-to-patient ratio stands at 1:40,000, and the loss of Dr Waiye not only deprives the province of a dedicated young professional but also threatens health service delivery if other doctors leave due to safety concerns.

"SiPHA is demanding a response and assurance within 48 hours," Dr Ken said.

Following the incident, Kundiawa General Hospital came to a total shutdown this morning.

Director of Curative Health Services, Joseph Ande, announced on behalf of hospital management and staff that all operations will cease for two days as a mark of respect for their fallen colleague, with only emergency cases to be attended to.

He said if the petition is not met within two days, management will decide on the next course of action.

Earlier, CEO Dr Kassi had advised staff to return to their workstations, but staff disagreed and resolved to go on strike.

item.title: 30 illegal guns surrendered in Hela
item.description: Thirty high-powered illegal firearms have been surrendered in Hela Province and publicly displayed in Tari during PNG's 51st Independence anniversary celebrations. The weapons were surrendered by 30 men as part of the voluntary firearms surrender programme.
item.content:encoded:
Thirty high-powered illegal firearms have been surrendered in Hela Province and publicly displayed in Tari during PNG's 51st Independence anniversary celebrations.

The weapons were surrendered by 30 men as part of the voluntary firearms surrender programme.

The event was attended by Prime Minister James Marape, Komo Hulia MP Daniel Tindipu, Koroba-Lake Kopiago MP William Bando, and various invited dignitaries.

Speaking at the gathering, Hela Governor Philip Undialu said PNGDF and police intelligence estimates roughly 500 factory-made illegal firearms remain in circulation across the province.

Governor Undialu commended Prime Minister Marape and Police Minister Sir John Pundari for initiating and extending the national gun surrender amnesty through December, crediting the extension for building momentum among local tribesmen to step forward.

With the amnesty window closing in December, he is urging firearm owners to surrender their weapons before law enforcement operations intensify.

The Governor issued a direct call to ward councilors, Local-Level Government (LLG) presidents, church pastors, and village elders to identify and report remaining firearm owners.

"Miracles will not happen on their own," Governor Undialu stated. "We have felt the deep pain of tribal fights that have destroyed our communities—forcing innocent mothers, children, and the elderly to seek refuge on foreign land. We must put an end to this."

He emphasized that rhetoric must match reality.

"Many times in our speeches, we say 'Hela will never be the same again.' Hela will truly never be the same again once we remove all 500 guns and enforce a total provincial ban on alcohol," he said.

Governor Undialu announced a mandatory assembly for all ward councilors across Hela Province at the Hulukumaiya Haus on December 7.

"Ward councilors who fail to attend will be viewed as actively opposing peace efforts and will face consequences," he stated.

To enforce accountability at the leadership level, Governor Undialu pledged to take a sworn oath on the Bible declaring he does not own a firearm, mirroring pledges made by other MPs.

"All 400 public servants in Hela Province will be required to take the same public oath," he said.

item.title: Adapt to change: Saroa
item.description: Prominent Port Moresby legal practitioner Nelson Saroa has called on Papua New Guineans to shift their mindsets as the nation steps beyond 51 years of independence and enters its next 50-year chapter. Speaking during an independence anniversary message, the principal of Nelson Lawyers said PNG's future progress hinges on a fundamental shift in perspective across all levels of society.
item.content:encoded:
Prominent Port Moresby legal practitioner Nelson Saroa has called on Papua New Guineans to shift their mindsets as the nation steps beyond 51 years of independence and enters its next 50-year chapter.

Speaking during an independence anniversary message, the principal of Nelson Lawyers said PNG's future progress hinges on a fundamental shift in perspective across all levels of society.

"My overall message for the Independence was a reminder to our people that the 51 years represents a new era," Saroa said.

"It's the next 50, and a positive mindset, a more progressive and motivated perspective, is now necessary for Papua New Guineans to start moving forward."

Saroa emphasised that leadership responsibility must extend beyond political institutions into everyday community structures. He urged leaders across professional sectors, youth groups, sporting codes, and local government wards, districts, and provinces to actively cultivate positive change.

"It's important that all leaders in all levels of society have a shift in their minds and are positive in promoting and motivating the next generation of our leaders and our people," he said.

Without this positive mindset and growth, Saroa warned, the country risks underutilising its vast potential.

"Without that positive mindset, without that positive growth, we won't be able to harness the full potential and full benefits of what this country has to offer."

Highlighting the rapid pace of global and domestic developments, Saroa stressed that nation-building starts at the grassroots level, within households, schools, and local communities where young people are raised and mentored.

"The world is changing, and we have to embrace the changes that are coming," Saroa said.

"Our ability to embrace, adapt, and create opportunities that are now presenting before us is now more important than ever. We must be able to embrace change, and with that, a more positive approach to life in general."

item.title: Panguna landowner’s commit to Lloyd’s Metals
item.description: Landowners from Panguna communities have united in a significant ceremony on Wednesday, [September 16], pledging renewed commitment to the Autonomous Bougainville Government’s plan to redevelop the Panguna Mine. The Panguna Landowner Interim Council, chiefs, and representatives from Guava, Dapera, Moroni and Pirurari offered heartfelt apologies to the government and developer Lloyds Panguna Metals
item.content:encoded:
Landowners from Panguna communities have united in a significant ceremony on Wednesday, [September 16], pledging renewed commitment to the Autonomous Bougainville Government’s plan to redevelop the Panguna Mine.

The Panguna Landowner Interim Council, chiefs, and representatives from Guava, Dapera, Moroni and Pirurari offered heartfelt apologies to the government and developer Lloyds Panguna Metals and Energy Limited [LPMEL] for the violent events of September 13.

Guava Chief Titus Miri, brother of the late Francis Ona, says his family now stands fully behind the redevelopment.

“My heartfelt apologies to Lloyds, you have invested so much, and our own people have done this. Shame on us. As a chief, I must defend my land, but what has happened has caused me great pain. Today I step down and give my full support to the government. No more games, let us move on and make things happen for Bougainville,” Miri said.

Stakeholders agreed to work closely with police and allow the law to take its course, while veterans pledged to support the process without violence.

LPMEL CEO Hulala Tokome appealed for reconciliation, stressing that destruction must never be the way forward.

“We have lost millions of kina worth of machinery, but violence cannot solve our differences.

"Lloyds is here for more than a mine, we want to create jobs, train young people, support health and education, build infrastructure, and sustainable communities. But we cannot do these things if property continues to be burned and fights continue.

"What has happened, has happened, we must move forward together,” Tokome said.

The ceremony was witnessed by ABG Veterans Minister Linus Dake Jr, the Member for Ioro Constituency David Miringtoro, Chief of Bougainville Police Service Deputy Commissioner Francis Tokura, veterans and community leaders.

Both drivers and bus crews were arr
item.content:encoded:
Police in Enga arrested 32 people for various summary offences as part of a major Independence law enforcement blitz across the province.

Acting Provincial Police Commander [PPC] Chief Inspector Daniel Yangen confirmed the arrests, which target reckless road behaviour, illegal gambling, public drunkenness, and drinking inside moving Public Motor Vehicles [PMVs]. Both drivers and bus crews were arrested for allowing passengers to consume alcohol on board.

Chief Inspector Yangen admitted that many of these summary offences had become normalised over the years due to lax law enforcement by police.

However, he assured the public that despite manpower shortages, he will strictly enforce the law at all levels during his tenure as Acting PPC and Wabag Police Station Commander.

In a direct warning to his own family and community members, Chief Inspector Yangen cautioned against relying on traditional ties to avoid prosecution. He warned that relatives attempting to use the wantok system for leniency would be charged with obstructing police duties.

Police have also announced strict bail conditions to deter offenders during the 51st Independence anniversary celebrations including; unlicensed sale of alcohol – K5,000 bail; public alcohol consumption and homebrew offences – K1,000 bail; illegal gambling including Bingo and card games – K1,000 bail; fighting in public places – K1,000 bail; and, cultivating, selling, or possessing marijuana – No bail.

While urging the public to celebrate the nation’s 51st Independence anniversary peacefully and responsibly, Chief Inspector Yangen stressed that police will maintain zero tolerance for lawlessness across Enga Province.

item.title: Forgotten by distance, not by patriotism
item.description: They may be far from the centres of power, but the people of Green River have once again shown that distance cannot diminish their love for Papua New Guinea.
